A standard paper or bioplastic cup with a special lid made of a good grade flexible polymer. Instead of having a raised nozzle or an open hole, the top of the cap has a cross shaped elastic membrane that remains firmly sealed by the tension of he material when no pressure is exarted. To drink, the user simply brings the glass close to the lips and exerts a slight downward pressure with the upper lip or tilts the glass. The membrane gives inward allowing the passage of the liquid only under the controlled contract of the lips. When the vessel is removed, the membrane instantly returns to its closed position, selaing the contents completely even if the vessel accidentally overturns

It consists of a doule layer short screw cap on the mouth of the glass. The top layer can gently rotate about 30 degrees with respect to the bottom layer by light manual twist using te fingers of the same hand that holds ther glass. Holding the body of the glass with yourfingers, the index finger or thumb is used to slightly rotate the upper section of the lid. When it is rotated, the internal holes that allow the passage of the coffee to a perimeter channel hidden under the upper edge of the glass are aligned. It can be drunk from any point of the outer circumference. When you turn the lid back to the top, it si completely blocked and impermeable to spills

The glass includes a concave hard lid. In the center of the concavity is a small integrated sliding disc that acts as an internal gate. This disc is connected to an internal low strength spring made of the same biodegradable plastic. The user holds the glass with one hand and, using the thumb of that same hand, lightly presses a side tab on the edge of the lid. This action displaces the internal gate millimeterly downwards, opening a hidden perimeter flow channel. The coffee flows towardsthe concave edge allowing you to drink from any angle of the circunference without the need to align a nozzle. When releasing the tab, the spring hermetically seals the outlet automatically

trials.description: There is a button on the handle that allows the liquid to seep through when you're ready to drink; otherwise, all the liquid sits in the inner layer, and the outer layer only holds liquid when holding the button and ready to drink. To refill, simply add liquid to the inner layer while holding the button.

So I added three different concepts and simple designs I just thought of. Number 2 is a cup with a simple cover you put on top, and then you have a tiny handle that you pull down to reveal the contents of the drink; of course, this idea is definitely not foolproof. Number three is very theoretical. I was wondering if you could make a cup with a thin film of a material that only dissolves based on our saliva and not the liquid inside; that way the liquid would stay inside. Now there is a theoretical way of doing this, but it's very hard and probably not a viable strategy. Finally, number 1 is the idea I was already experimenting with earlier, so it's a cup with an inner compartment that contains the liquid, but said liquid can only come out when the user holds the button, which will release the liquid to the outer layer. Now I have made it so there are tiny holes with micropumps that will release the liquid through the inner layer to the outer layer; of course, this is a complicated idea and not very viable as a disposable material. Also, the cup wouldn't be able to hold too much liquid, as the outer layer needs to be a somewhat decent size to hold the liquid when released so the user can drink. I ended up choosing idea number one.

trials.description: So the main idea is to lay the bike completely flat on its side on the car roof to reduce wind resistance. We'll use two rectangular mounts: the front one will be high (at a 3X height) and the rear one will be much lower (at an X height). The front mount will have a shallow cutout just to cradle the handlebar neck, while the rest of the handlebars will hang outside in the air, and we'll secure the neck in place with a rubber strap or lock. The rear mount will have a deeper cutout to support the back wheel. The clever part here is that the height difference creates a tilt that makes the bike lean backward, but since the handlebar is anchored in the front mount, it acts like a natural lock that stops the bike from sliding or shifting at all. Of course, the base height of the mounts makes sure no part of the bike or the pedals ever touches or scratches the car roof. And to make it super stable with no rattling or bouncing, we'll line the cutouts where the bike rests with a high-friction fabric to completely kill any slipping.
